en: (Niraupamyastava 238) ... [He] obtains a body that is incomparable, resembling the primary elements and their derivatives, with all its limbs variegated by various forms, and fully developed.

That body, which pervades the circles of assemblies in all Buddha-fields, is called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because it has reached the realization of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).
When mind, intellect, and consciousness no longer function,
one then attains the mind-made body and the stage of a Buddha.
Because of this statement,
the Blessed One is beyond comparison; likewise,

he is entirely free from the conceptualizations, perceptions, and mental constructions of mind and consciousness, ungrasped, equal to space, having entered into the nature of open space, and has attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
It is said: "In this regard,

noble sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva endowed with such patience, from the very moment of attaining the Immovable Bodhisattva stage, enters the profound dwelling of a bodhisattva, which is difficult to understand and undifferentiated."
Through such statements as "free from all signs," he understands the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature.

Having thus attained this patient acceptance (*kṣānti*), wherever that bodhisattva approaches—whether to an assembly of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, gods, or brahmās; or to an assembly of monks, nuns, heretics, or Māras—[he remains unshaken].
He approaches everywhere without hesitation and speaks with total confidence.
Why is that?

Because, through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), he has thoroughly penetrated all things in every way by means of the aspect of the non-arising of all phenomena.
Because he has no timidity before the assembly caused by ignorance or caused by afflictions, he has attained fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
By means of sustaining a lifespan for an inexpressibly inexpressible number of eons, he attains mastery over life (*āyur-vaśitā*);
and by means of entering the knowledge that realizes immeasurable and incalculable meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), he attains mastery over the mind (*ceto-vaśitā*).

Mastery over requisites, by manifesting the empowerment that adorns all world-systems with manifold arrays of ornaments; mastery over karma, by manifesting the empowerment of the maturation of karma according to the appropriate time;
and mastery over rebirth, by manifesting rebirth in all world-systems.

And he attains mastery over resolve by manifesting the appearance of Buddhas filling all world-systems; he attains mastery over aspiration by manifesting the attainment of perfect awakening in any Buddha-field or world as desired;
and he attains mastery over supernatural power by manifesting miraculous transformations in all Buddha-fields.
He attains mastery over phenomena by manifesting the illumination of the gateways to the Dharma, which are without end or middle;
and he attains mastery over gnosis by manifesting the perfect awakening to the powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities of a Buddha, the primary marks, and the secondary signs.

Thus, you who have attained these ten masteries are intent on the welfare of this world that is fallen into wrong views; by this, both his praiseworthy practice and his immeasurability and state of mindlessness are described.
In all that is to be explained hereafter, the threefold meaning should be applied to each [term].
For this very reason, it was said by the Blessed One:
"By those who have reached the perfection of patience regarding the profound Dharma and have attained fearlessness..."
It has been said, "those skilled in the detailed exposition of the discernment of phenomena.

In this context, phenomena (*dharma*) are of four kinds: the phenomena of insight (*vipaśyanā*), such as the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields; the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*), such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*), such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*); and the phenomena of realization (*adhigama-dharma*), such as the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), respectively.
By way of this distinction, four verses have been stated.

Among them, the Buddha-eye is produced through the formative activity of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-abhisaṃskāra*) and is comprised within the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), because it is attainable through the eightfold purification (*parikarman*) of the Stage of Youth (*kumārabhūmi*). Furthermore, the purification for these consists in the non-apprehension of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-anupalambha*).
Thus, it is not possible for even you to see anything with that eye, let alone with the others;
because the true reality does not come within the range of manifestation of any of the five eyes,
the knowledge of seeing is the non-seeing of all phenomena— this is the vision of the true reality.
One might object: "Even noble ones (*ārya*) who have attained the first stage and so forth do not perceive any phenomenon; what, then, is the superiority of this [attainment]?
To this he says: "And it is unsurpassed (*anuttarā*)," because in this state one does not emerge from the vision of the reality of things (*tattvārtha*).
The previous seven dwellings are mixed, whereas this one is entirely pure.
As it has been said:
"When, moreover, having abandoned all preparatory practice, one has passed from the seventh stage to the eighth stage, then, having mounted the completely pure Bodhisattva vehicle," and so forth.
Therefore, because there is no other dwelling of the bodhisattvas more profound than these profound ones, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) in this context.

Discernment is [to be understood] by way of its characteristic, its function, its cause, its fruit, its enumeration, its gratification, its disadvantage, its escape, and by way of affliction, purification, thorough knowledge, abandonment, realization, and cultivation. In that regard, there are six [aspects] in their respective order.
By means of specific meanings,
one [form] is comprised of two meanings, and likewise another; one by one, and the other by two,
you manifest transformations through great supernatural power and the illusion-like samādhi.
Because of such statements as these;
furthermore, there is one [element] by way of its cultivation (bhāvanā).
In that context, "formless" (arūpavat) means like space (ākāśavat).
And so it has been said: "To such an extent that he displays the color and form of the Tathāgata’s body for those beings who are to be disciplined by the Tathāgata.

Thus indeed, O Son of the Victor, however many are the ranges of birthplaces and inclinations of beings throughout the inexpressible expansions of Buddha-fields, in each and every one of them the Tathāgata displays a manifestation of his own body."
He is free from all conceptualizations and perceptions regarding the body and has attained the nature of space.
Furthermore, this manifestation of his body is unfailing and not in vain for the sake of maturing and disciplining all sentient beings, and so forth.
In terms of classification, there are four [bodies]; regarding the distinction of the three bodies, there are three verses.
For instance, on the seventh stage, one knows the array of the Buddha-body (*buddhakāyavyūha*), yet at that time one is not yet able to bring it to completion.

However, through the knowledge of the array of the Buddha-body on that stage, one knows the desire to bring it to completion. From this stage onward, one brings it to completion; this is to be understood from such sources as the *Āryadaśabhūmika*.
It has been stated that there is the "complete pacification of the obstructions of karma.
Upon the simultaneous attainment of this very patience (*kṣānti*), whatever karmic obstructions he possesses that would ripen as rebirths in good or bad destinies are completely severed for him.

This is with the exception of those [obstructions] pertaining to the Tathāgatas, which arise from their compassionate regard for future generations; therefore, there is a verse regarding this distinction:
The overflow of karma (*karmapluti*) is the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of karma;
because the mind does not deviate from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
there are three [types] according to the designation of speech and body.
In that regard, it is eternal because of the departure from arising; it is stable because of the departure from cessation; it is auspicious because of the absence of duality;
and its auspiciousness arises from the non-conceptualization of duality—according to this statement, there is one skill.
In that regard, the absence of conceit results from the transformation of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*);
the absence of conceptual construction results from the transformation of the active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*);
and the absence of movement results from the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

In all [the preceding sections], by means of summarizing the three topics established therein and through the glorification of the Blessed One’s qualities, this [verse] is spoken as one for the purpose of dedicating the merit produced to the establishment of sentient beings upon this earth.

In that regard, he is the "Well-Gone" (*sugata*) because of his excellent departure and because he does not return. He is "inconceivable" (*acintya*) because he is beyond the scope of logic, inexpressible, and due to his noble gnosis; he is "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) because he has attained mastery through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which is itself immeasurable.

For in this stage, the bodhisattva, established in the meditative concentrations of the continuous application for the realization of great enlightenment, possesses an intellect that is perpetually ablaze like fire in the accomplishment of tasks,
and yet remains at all times absorbed in peaceful dhyāna attainments.
Thus it has been said. This concludes the summary of the second [chapter].
Now, concerning the third stage of the dwelling, the *Acintyastava* says:

"If the establishment of a thing were to exist by way of its own nature, like the establishment of the extinction of a lamp that has been blown out, then how could there be the pacification of delusion, which acts as the great lord of all afflictions?"
Therefore, he stated that dependent phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) in order to abandon all views in every respect; thus he spoke these words and so forth.
In that regard, on the ninth Bodhisattva stage, there is the dwelling in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvidvihāra*).
In this regard, a bodhisattva, being dissatisfied even with that profound dwelling and pursuing further excellence of knowledge,

understands as it truly is all those mental formations of the knowledge of phenomena by which a bodhisattva must teach the Dharma to others in all its aspects, as well as the entire task of proclaiming the Dharma.
In this regard, this is the function of the exposition of the Dharma:
[it concerns] those who are afflicted and those who are purified within the dense ranges of mental activity; that by which they are afflicted and purified;
what constitutes affliction and purification; its non-exclusive nature; and its both exclusive and non-exclusive nature.
His knowledge is according to reality (*yathābhūtajñāna*).

Furthermore, regarding that which constitutes his state as a great Dharma-preacher in all its aspects—belonging to one who is skilled in teaching and skilled in the performance of teaching—it should be understood in detail exactly as in the Sūtra.
As for "unequaled knowledge," because he abides in the activity of a Tathāgata on the tenth stage, it is as stated in the *Āryadaśabhūmika*.

"Up until the end of ten hundred thousand incalculable hundreds of thousands of samādhis, the bodhisattva-samādhi called 'Possessing the Consecration of the Distinctive Wisdom of Omniscience' becomes manifest," and so forth;
concerning which it was said:
"By the force of previous momentum and through the departure of all conceptual constructions, he [attains it]."
Furthermore, he does not exert effort for the sake of maturing embodied beings;
rather, in whatever way, by whatever means, and in whatever manner a person is to be disciplined,
he [acts] accordingly through both teaching and the form-body, or through conduct and deportment.
Thus, for one whose intellect is always unimpeded, the welfare of sentient beings proceeds effortlessly throughout the world as far as the limits of space.
Having reached this state, the Bodhisattva is equal to the Tathāgatas.

He attains equality toward all worlds in regard to the deliverance of sentient beings. (4) Now, whatever the difference may be between a minute atom and the earth, or between the water in a cow’s footprint and the great ocean—that is the difference between Bodhisattvas and a Buddha. (5) Thus it is said.

(Css 244) Regarding "inconceivable," as it has been said: "O Son of the Victor, indeed, a bodhisattva who has thus entered this stage attains the bodhisattva liberation called 'Inconceivable' and the 'Unobstructed,' and so forth."

Regarding those qualities which are far beyond the range of speech and are indeed inaccessible to words, it is said in the *Bhagavatī*—in the section describing the qualities of the bodhisattva established on the stage of reaching the ultimate—that "as many atoms as there would be in all the worlds rolled into one, so many are his qualities here in the tenth [stage]. This is stated as being beyond illustration.

By means of eight similes—likening phenomena to an illusion, a mirage, a gandharva city, the moon in water, a dream, a reflection, an echo, and a magical creation—the eight characteristics of the bodhisattva’s conviction in these phenomena are indicated.

Namely: the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of the imagined (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of the dependent (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).
Among these, three characteristics have been taught in sequence by means of six, six, and three [factors], according to the distinctions of teaching, function, and meaning.
The summary of these very three is by means of one [verse]; the remaining [categories] should be understood through six, seven, six, and seven [verses].
Thus, by means of the seven verses beginning with "by way of similes such as illusion," there is a summary of all [the qualities] by way of describing their attributes in due order;
for, according to your view, this dwelling has attained a certain inconceivable and supremely profound state.
One [verse] is for the purpose of demonstrating that they bring you into existence in this very way.
Another [type of dedication] is the dedication of merit for the purpose of establishing sentient beings upon this very earth.
The summarized meaning of the third [section].
(Css 245) In the *Paramārthastava*,
beginning from the state of fruition, all untainted (*anāśrava*) phenomena, having attained every form of unsurpassed purity, receive the designation "Perfectly Awakened One" (*saṃbuddha*).
Since even at the stage of their cause they are not empty, how much more so at the stage of their fruit; thus he says:
"How shall I praise you, O Protector? and so forth;

this indicates the section beginning with "unborn and without abode" (*anutpannam anālayam*), meaning "by way of an unborn intrinsic nature," and ending with "homage be to you, the profound one" (*gambhīrāya namo 'stu te*).
Speech and the path of words, as well as volition—by which [the Buddha] has transcended the range of these two;
thus it is said: "inconceivable and invisible."
The response by way of conventional truth is given with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) and so forth.

From the stage of *Abhimukhī* onwards, because [the bodhisattva] has specifically attained [qualities] such as non-arising (*anutpāda*), there are five [aspects] in the sense of being unsurpassed; and from that stage onward, because of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*), there is one [aspect] in the sense of supreme profundity, since even the remaining latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obscurations are no longer present.
When you have been praised in this way, may you be "praised"—this is the ellipsis, meaning "conventionally" (*saṃvṛtyā*). Alternatively, what indeed has been praised in the ultimate sense?

The word *kiṃ* is used in the sense of negation (*ākṣepe*), and the word *bata* functions as a particle of emphasis (*avadhāraṇenaiva*). He explains that very point with the verse beginning "By praise," and so forth.
Now, demonstrating that even from the perspective of conventional reality praise is impossible, he says:
"Who is able to praise you? and so forth.
The Blessed One is devoid of arising and ceasing, whereas the praiser is possessed of arising and ceasing.
The Blessed One is without beginning, middle, or end;
yet he is comprised within the dependent origination of the three sections.
The Blessed One is liberated from the grasper and the grasped, yet he moves within both the grasper and the grasped.
Even from the perspective of conventional truth, praise in the form of proclaiming real qualities is impossible;
for even though the two truths exist, there is an absence of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) due to the reality of inconceivable dependent origination.
However, one who proceeds by means of the conviction in the intrinsic purity [of phenomena] through the non-apprehension of the entity possesses great fruit;
thus it should be understood that a great impossibility [of falling back] occurs.
One [type of dedication] is for the purpose of dedicating merit toward the attainment of the state of a Sugata.

It should be understood that it is precisely with reference to this much of the subject matter that the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya-krama*) is taught in detail in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other scriptures.
Thus concludes the summary of the meaning of the fourth [chapter].
This is the summary of the meaning of the *Catuḥstava* by Paṇḍita Amṛtākara.
